clue.text: Stop getting drunk in English pubs, or silly

indicators.note: 'in' tells us the English abbreviation sits among the other letters being mixed
something silly is muddled and nonsensical, so the letters it describes are thrown out of order

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
taken as written, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: A drinker is urged to stop boozing in English pubs before making a fool of themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: To sober up is to become clear-headed again, which means ceasing to be intoxicated.

clue.text: Indicating subscription required

blocks.note: first meaning: showing something by gestures or signals
second meaning: the act of writing your name at the foot of a document, which a subscription needs

explanation.surface: A notice says that joining or renewing requires payment.
explanation.walkthrough: To subscribe originally meant to write one's name underneath, so the act a subscription calls for is putting your name to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Making gestures to point something out is one sense; putting a name on a document is the other.

clue.text: Legally constrained, it's clear

blocks.note: first meaning: ordered by a British court to keep the peace, on pain of forfeiting a sum
second meaning: to leap over an obstacle, as a horse clears a fence

explanation.surface: A legal restriction has been placed on someone, and the position is plain.
explanation.walkthrough: In British courts, being bound over means being placed under a court order to behave; the same words describe springing over a hurdle.
explanation.definitionFit: A magistrate's order restrains someone's conduct, and leaping across a barrier is to jump it cleanly.

clue.text: Fabric providing a little light covering

blocks.note: a ray is a thin beam, a small amount of light
on can mean over or covering, as a lid is on a jar

explanation.surface: A thin cloth lets some daylight through when used as a cover.
explanation.definitionFit: Rayon is a manufactured cloth made from cellulose fibres, often used as a silk substitute.

clue.text: Journalists go north of the border to apply coercion

blocks.note: the press is journalists collectively
gang is the Scots word for go; north of the border means in Scotland

explanation.surface: Reporters head to Scotland to put pressure on someone.
explanation.walkthrough: For British writers, 'north of the border' means Scotland, so the clue asks for the Scottish form of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To press-gang someone is to force them into doing something, as naval gangs once forced men into service.

clue.text: Get father to betray where uncle is

blocks.note: pop is an informal word for father; 'Get' just fetches him
to shop someone is slang for informing on them

explanation.surface: Someone persuades their dad to inform on the relative who has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncle' is old slang for a pawnbroker, so the uncle here is not a relative; a pop shop is a pawnshop, from 'pop' meaning to pawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A pawnbroker, nicknamed uncle, works from a pawnshop, which slang calls a pop shop.

clue.text: A couple of Greek characters work for church

blocks.note: two letters of the Greek alphabet, pi and eta, side by side

explanation.surface: Two people from Greece take on a job for their local church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' looks like people; it means letters of an alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A pietà is a painting or sculpture of the Virgin Mary holding the dead Christ, often made for churches.

clue.text: Greek warrior a sculptor sculpted

indicators.note: sculpting shapes material into a new form, so the letters are remodelled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An artist carves a statue of a hero from ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: Patroclus is the companion of Achilles in Homer's Iliad, killed fighting at Troy.

clue.text: Ran like certain animals, some of which are deranged

indicators.note: 'some of' takes only a part of the following words, so the letters sit inside them

blocks.note: found running across the three words

explanation.surface: A herd of beasts bolts, and several of them seem to have gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods to the mad March hare.
explanation.definitionFit: To hare is to run very fast, the way the long-eared animals do.

clue.text: Direction-finder for missile

blocks.note: first meaning: the Pole Star, used by navigators to find north
second meaning: a submarine-launched nuclear missile of the Cold War

explanation.surface: A guidance system is fitted to a rocket.
explanation.definitionFit: The North Star has long guided travellers, and the same name was given to a ballistic weapon.

clue.text: Loud celebration in college

blocks.note: first meaning: showy and garish, as loud colours are
second meaning: a reunion feast for old members of an Oxford or Cambridge college

explanation.surface: A noisy party is under way at a university college.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one noisy party; in fact the adjective and the noun are separate meanings of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Garish clothes are called loud, and Oxford colleges hold an annual dinner for former students called a gaudy.

clue.text: Prince Albert seen about voting

blocks.note: the Electors were the German princes who chose the Holy Roman Emperor
Al is the short form of the name Albert

explanation.surface: Queen Victoria's consort is spotted hovering around a polling station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince Albert' looks like one person, but it splits into two pieces, and 'about' belongs to the definition rather than signalling a container.
explanation.definitionFit: Electoral describes anything concerning elections, the process by which people cast votes.

clue.text: Units invading one Eastern country or another

indicators.note: an invader moves inside a territory, so one word is placed within the other

blocks.note: an Asian nation, which takes the other letters inside it
ones are single units

explanation.surface: Military units invade an Asian nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the single word 'another', meaning another Eastern country, so the clue's wordplay supplies one Asian nation and the answer is a second.
explanation.definitionFit: Indonesia, the archipelago republic of South-East Asia, is a further Eastern nation besides the first one named.

clue.text: Communist Party's comeback is more surprising

indicators.note: a comeback returns the way it came, so the letters are read from the end

blocks.note: red is the traditional label for a communist
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: A revived Communist Party would surprise political observers.
explanation.definitionFit: Something odder is stranger, so it causes greater astonishment than something ordinary.

clue.text: One − volume there's little information about, in fact

indicators.note: 'about' means surrounding, so the information goes around the other letters

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information, short for general information
I is the Roman numeral one
V is the abbreviation for volume

explanation.surface: Someone is insisting that one book holds hardly any information at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The I and V sit together inside GEN. 'In fact' looks like a phrase, but 'in' just links and the definition is the noun 'fact'.
explanation.definitionFit: A given is something taken as known and certain, a basic truth used as a starting point.

clue.text: Foreign drama is unsatisfactory without directions - such as this one?

indicators.note: 'without' here means outside, so two pieces wrap around the compass letters

blocks.note: No (or Noh) is traditional Japanese theatre
taken as written
E and S, east and south, two compass points
off means not up to standard, as in an off day

explanation.surface: A critic complains that a foreign play is poor because it lacks stage directions.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points back at 'directions': noises off is a stage direction for sounds made offstage, and also the title of Michael Frayn's farce.
explanation.definitionFit: A script's instruction for sounds heard from the wings is a typical stage direction, so it is one example.

clue.text: Thief Lucy disturbed breaking into cars

indicators.note: a burglar breaking into something gets inside it, so the mixed name goes within the other word
disturbed things are knocked out of their proper place, so the name's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: autos are cars
the name rearranged

explanation.surface: A criminal named Lucy is interrupted while breaking into parked cars.
explanation.walkthrough: Autolycus is the rogue and pickpocket in Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale, named after a thief of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Autolycus is a famous literary and mythological rogue who steals for a living.

clue.text: Collection for union negotiator

blocks.note: surface reading: money or support gathered for a trade-union official at the bargaining table
setter's reading: the union is a marriage, and the collection is the bride's stock of clothes and linen she brings to it

explanation.surface: Workers pass round the hat for the official who bargains on their behalf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' suggests a trade union; it is a wedding, and the person entering into it is the one the collection is for.
explanation.definitionFit: A bride traditionally assembles clothes and household linen ahead of her marriage; that gathered set has a French name.

clue.text: Person seeking views for painting raised the matter

indicators.note: in a down answer, something raised is lifted upward, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: a canvas is an oil painting
res is Latin for thing or matter, familiar from legal phrases

explanation.surface: Someone asks for opinions on an artwork that has brought up the issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Views' looks like scenery to paint; it means opinions.
explanation.definitionFit: A canvasser goes door to door asking people their opinions or their voting intentions.

clue.text: Boldness proving misguided in occasional reverse

indicators.note: 'in' places the mistaken word inside the other one
putting something into reverse makes it go backwards, so its letters run from the end

blocks.note: odd means occasional, as in odd jobs; it is turned round and split open
erring means going astray or making mistakes

explanation.surface: Courage turns out to be a mistake when someone occasionally backs down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasional reverse' looks like a phrase about retreat, but 'occasional' is the word to turn round.
explanation.definitionFit: Derring-do is an old-fashioned word for daring, heroic action, which is the same as boldness.

clue.text: Work - as it gets distributed among many females

indicators.note: things distributed are spread about, so the two short words are mixed up
'among' sets the mixed letters inside the surrounding pieces

blocks.note: D is the Roman numeral 500, a large number
the two words rearranged
F is female; doubling it makes it plural

explanation.surface: A job is shared out among a large group of women.
explanation.walkthrough: The distaff, the staff that holds wool for spinning, stood for women's work, hence 'the distaff side' for the female line.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinning on the distaff was the traditional household labour of women, so the word came to mean that labour.

clue.text: Irish playwright said to compose poetry

indicators.note: 'said' means spoken, so the word is judged by how it sounds rather than its spelling

blocks.note: poets are traditionally said to sing their verses

explanation.surface: An Irish dramatist is reported to write verse too.
explanation.walkthrough: J. M. Synge wrote The Playboy of the Western World; his name is pronounced like the verb for making music with the voice.
explanation.definitionFit: John Millington Synge was a leading dramatist of the Irish literary revival.

clue.text: Dramatic performance in final part of board meeting

blocks.note: first meaning: Samuel Beckett's one-act play
second meaning: the last stage of a chess game, when the two sides meet over the board

explanation.surface: Someone causes a scene at the end of a company directors' gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board meeting' suggests company directors; it is a chess game, played across a board.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's play bears this title, and chess players use the term for the closing phase of play.

clue.text: Try, for example, to make one's mark

blocks.note: first meaning: a try in rugby is one kind of points-winning play
second meaning: to cut or scratch a line into a surface

explanation.surface: Someone attempts to make a name for themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' looks like a verb meaning attempt; it is the rugby noun, where touching the ball down behind the line earns points.
explanation.definitionFit: A rugby try is an example of a points tally, and incising a line is also to score something.

clue.text: It can give actors no end of excitement!

indicators.note: 'no end of' says the final letter of the next word is to be taken away
something that can give is not rigid and will bend into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the closing letter, which is removed

explanation.surface: An award ceremony thrills performers enormously.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: winning an Academy Award brings actors endless excitement.
explanation.definitionFit: 'It' points to the thing described by the rest of the clue, the Hollywood statuette awarded for film acting.

clue.text: After course, watch the port going West!

indicators.note: 'After' sets the order: the second item comes behind the first in the answer

blocks.note: fish is a course in a formal meal
to guard is to keep watch over

explanation.surface: After a sailing course, someone watches the harbour as a ship heads west.
explanation.walkthrough: Fishguard is a harbour town in west Wales, where ferries leave westward for Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishguard is a Welsh harbour town whose ferries sail west across the Irish Sea to Rosslare.

clue.text: Moth, for example, is just the end in drapery

indicators.note: 'the end in' picks out only the closing letter of the next word

blocks.note: fair means just or even-handed
only its last letter is kept

explanation.surface: A moth caught in the curtains has only its tail end showing.
explanation.walkthrough: Moth is one of Titania's fairy attendants in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, not an insect here.
explanation.definitionFit: Moth is the name of a supernatural sprite serving the fairy queen in Shakespeare's comedy.

clue.text: From Germany originally, rampaging host

indicators.note: 'originally' means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept
a rampaging crowd runs wild in disorder, so its letters are scrambled

blocks.note: its first letter
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A marauding army sweeps out of Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a host here is an army.
explanation.definitionFit: The Goths were Germanic tribes whose armies overran large parts of the Roman Empire.

clue.text: Person who's withdrawn from race, tho' in form

indicators.note: to put something in a new form is to reshape it, so the letters take a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, the comma and apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: An athlete pulls out of a race even though they are on good form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In form' reads as a phrase about fitness, but 'in' belongs to the letters being rearranged and 'form' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An anchorite is a religious hermit who has retired from society to live in seclusion.

clue.text: This miss could be turned to advantage

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: an asset is a benefit or advantage

explanation.surface: A young woman's setback might yet work out in her favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a failure; it means a girl, and the answer is a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Tessa is a female first name, so it can name a young woman addressed as Miss.

clue.text: Dismiss shrewd and brilliant six-footer

blocks.note: to fire someone is to dismiss them from a job
fly is British slang for sharp or knowing

explanation.surface: A boss sacks a clever, gifted and very tall employee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' suggests a tall person; it is an insect, which has six legs, and 'brilliant' means glowing.
explanation.definitionFit: A firefly is a beetle that gives off light, and like every insect it walks on six legs.

clue.text: In periods of prosperity yen shows rapid rise

blocks.note: good times are the ups in ups and downs
a yen is a longing or urge

explanation.surface: During a boom the Japanese currency climbs sharply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' looks like the Japanese money; it means a desire.
explanation.definitionFit: An upsurge is a sudden, sharp increase in something such as prices or activity.
